1. The animation shows inflation eroding what a fixed income annuity check can buy. A character named Ruth gets a check, drawn as a row of crates that stands for what the check buys. The labels say "US consumer prices (CPI-U)", "ILLUSTRATIVE" and "US only · history, not a forecast".

2. The row of crates changes across the frames. In frames 1–4 the row stretches out, and the last crate is dark in the first frame. By frames 5–6, Ruth is labeled "age 85" and the caption reads "check: +2% a year". Nine crates are bright and one is dark, and the label says "about 9 in 10". The bracket "first check: 10 crates" marks the starting purchasing power.

3. It means that when prices rise about 2% a year, a check that was worth 10 crates at the start buys only about 9 crates' worth by age 85. The bracket and label suggest a loss of roughly one-tenth. The "+2% a year" caption could be read two ways. It could mean the check grows 2% a year while prices grow faster. It could also mean prices rise 2% a year. The image doesn't make this clear, so I can't say for sure which is meant.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer could take away that a flat payout loses buying power over time. They might then weigh a payout option that adjusts for inflation against a level one. The image doesn't recommend either choice.

5. That takeaway is my own conclusion, not something the animation states. The animation only shows the shrinking purchasing power. It also says it is illustrative and a history, not a forecast.
